pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the development office in this workspace. Share it with the executive director, the gift officers, whoever processes gifts and the events coordinator.
: every individual, family, business, foundation and faith group, with their steward, giving level, recurring gift, how they like to be contacted and the next planned touch.
: every gift and pledge payment, with method, campaign, gift type, tribute and the thank-you letter that went out.
: promises to give over time, with the payment schedule, what has been paid and what is still owed.
: each appeal, gala, giving day or capital project, with its goal and progress.
: thank-you calls, visits, updates and asks, each with a due date.
Gifts are recorded the day they arrive and thanked within two days.
Pledge payments due this week get a friendly reminder.
Stewards work their follow-ups: calls, visits and updates.
On Friday the director reviews the Dashboard: received, pledged, unthanked gifts and campaign progress.
Every morning: Gifts waiting for a thank-you
Every Monday: follow-ups due this week and pledge payments due
Every month: recurring gifts with a declined card, lapsed donors to win back
Every January: year-end receipts for every donor who gave last year
Giving amounts and contact details are marked confidential. Share the workspace with staff and board members who need it, and never export a donor list for anyone outside the office.

The director of development owns campaign goals and the major-gift list. Gift officers steward their own donors and keep follow-ups current. The person who processes gifts records, matches and thanks. The events coordinator logs every guest who gives at an event as a donor, so nobody is thanked twice or missed.

Rename campaigns, gift types and acknowledgment letters to match your organization, then delete the sample rows once your own are in. Any cell can be edited in place, cards drag between columns, and every total updates on its own.
Development at a glance. Charts read the live tables, so they move as gifts are recorded.

text.text: A gift is processed the same day it arrives and thanked within 48 hours. Donors who are thanked quickly give again far more often than donors who wait two weeks for a letter.
Every gift, the same five steps
Open the donor (or add them), then add the gift: amount, method, campaign, and the gift type. A check gets its check number in the notes; a card or online gift gets the processor's receipt number.
If the gift pays toward a promise, link it to the pledge in
update by themselves. If an employer will match it, add a second gift of type
. The received date is stamped and the donor's lifetime total moves.

: a standard letter for most gifts, a personal note from the director above your major-gift line, a tribute card when someone gave in honor or memory of another person, or no letter when the donor asked to stay anonymous.
Send it and press Mark thanked.

In the United States, any single gift of $250 or more needs a written acknowledgment that names the amount and says whether the donor received anything in return. Put that sentence in every letter so you never have to think about it. Donors who give through the year get one year-end receipt in January listing every gift.
When a gift is made in honor or memory of someone, write the person's name in
. Send the donor their thank-you and send a card to the family or the honoree. Never mention the amount on the family's card.
Monthly and quarterly donors are your steadiest income. When a card is declined, set

to Card declined and call or email within a week; most lapsed monthly gifts are simply expired cards. Thank recurring donors once a year with a note about what their year of giving did, not with twelve letters.
Dashboard: every received gift is thanked
Deposits match the gifts recorded this week
Pledge payments due in the next seven days have had their reminder

A check for $1,000 arrives from a donor who pledged $4,000 over a year. The gift processor records it as a pledge payment linked to her pledge, marks it received, chooses the director's note, and the director signs it that afternoon. The pledge now shows $3,000 still owed and the next payment due in three months.
Stewardship is everything that happens between asks. The aim is simple: every donor should hear what their money did before they hear the next request.
Plan about seven touches a year for each major and mid-level donor, and only one or two of them are asks. The rest are thank-yous, updates, invitations and small personal notes. Put each one in
with a due date and the steward who owns it.
(lifetime giving $5,000 and up): a named steward, a visit or call each quarter, a personal update from the program team twice a year.
($500 to $4,999): a call after each gift, an invitation to see the work, a year-end note from the director.
(under $500): a prompt letter, the newsletter, and an invitation to give monthly.

Call within a week of a first gift. Board members are great at this: a two-minute call that says only thank you, with no ask, is the single best thing you can do to bring a donor back.

A donor is lapsed when they have not given in about 14 months. Before you ask again, send something about what their last gift did. Ask what they care about now; some have moved, some have changed causes, and some were waiting to be asked.
on the donor. Some want mail, some email, some a phone call, and some want no solicitations at all. Honor it every time; a donor who asked for no calls and gets one is a donor you lose.
Open the Follow-ups that are due this week and overdue
Make the thank-you calls for last week's first-time donors
Send one program update with a photo to your top ten donors
Move donors whose next touch has passed to a new date

A business gave $2,000 to last winter's drive and has not given since. The steward sends a short email with a photo of the families the drive served, then calls a week later to invite the owner to the harvest supper. The owner comes, meets a family, and gives $3,000 to the spring appeal.
A campaign is a goal, a deadline and a list of people who will be asked. Plan it on paper first; the Campaigns table then keeps score.

Start with what you need to fund and what you raised last time. A good goal is a stretch, not a wish: last year's total plus 10 to 20 percent for an annual appeal. For a capital project, secure about half of the goal in large gifts and pledges before you announce it publicly.

Write down how many gifts of each size you need. A common shape: the top gift is about a tenth of the goal, the next two together are another tenth, and about 80 percent of the money comes from the top 20 percent of donors. Match real names from Donors to each line before the campaign goes live.

A business that agrees to match gifts up to a set amount gives donors a reason to give now. Record the business's promise as a pledge on the campaign, and its payment as a matching gift when it arrives.
A results note to all donors within two weeks
A short write-up for next year: what worked, who gave for the first time, what to change

The youth center roof needs $60,000. The director secures a $25,000 foundation pledge and a $10,000 business pledge in the quiet phase, then goes public. Six weeks later the campaign shows $41,500 given and pledged, and a giving day challenge closes the gap.
